title: credible interpretability evidence of deceptive internal ...

topic.original: credible interpretability evidence of deceptive internal representations is sufficient grounds for a mandatory deployment halt, even absent any harmful output.
topic.final: credible interpretability evidence of deceptive internal representations is sufficient grounds for a mandatory deployment halt, even absent any harmful output.
topic.background: Doctrinal basis: This inverts the ordinary structure: liability on mens rea alone, with no actus reus. Criminal law refuses this (no thought-crime), but preventive regimes — quarantine, civil commitment, material-support statutes — do act on dangerous internal states before any act. The motion asks which template governs.

scope.core_proposition: Whether reliable mechanistic interpretability evidence of deceptive internal model states justifies a mandatory halt to AI deployment, even if no harmful outputs have been observed.
on_scope_evidence: historical instances of deceptive alignment in models
false positive rates in interpretability tools
causal links between internal representations and outputs
key_tensions: precautionary halting on internal evidence (safetyist) vs requiring demonstrable harm to justify halting (accelerationist)
reliability of interpretability tools (skeptic) vs treating internal deception as a smoking gun (safetyist)
burden of proof for deployment: guilty until proven innocent (safetyist) vs innocent until proven guilty (accelerationist/skeptic)
off_scope_topics: general AI capabilities and scaling laws
drift_signatures: shifting from internal representations to output-based harms or jailbreaks
debating the general philosophy of AI regulation without connecting to interpretability evidence
discussing model capabilities rather than internal deceptive states
focusing on the economic cost of halting deployment rather than the sufficiency of the evidence
scope.example_ceiling: Deployment-level decisions for frontier AI models; regulatory interventions and corporate governance decisions. Examples should focus on internal model states and deployment policies, not physical world catastrophic harm.
